# Up-Sampling {#sec-imbalenced-upsample}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Up-Sampling
:::

Upsampling is one of the conceptually easiest ways to handle imbalanced data.
Like all other methods in this section, it is a supervised method,
since it requires knowledge of the outcome.
This also means that it can only be applied to the training data set,
since we need the outcome.
See also [down-dampling](imbalenced-downsample.qmd), which is the opposite action.

The algorithm is quite simple.
Tally the number of observations within each class, as well as keep track of which observations are associated with each class.
The class with the most observations is then denoted as the majority class,
The remaining classes are denoted as the minority classes.
The observations of each minority class are then sampled with replacement to increase the number of observations in the class.
Typically, to align with the number of observations with that of the majority class.

One could also modify this for a different threshold,
say 80%, which would make all minority classes with less than 80% of the number of observations of the majority class,
upsample until they have at least 80% of that of the majority class.

This action can drastically increase the number of observations depending on the number of minority classes and the ratio between them.
A 90-10 split would result in a 80% increase in data, and a 90-5-5 split would result in a 170% increase.
No data is being deleted in this modification as we are just adding more rows, which are duplicates of existing rows.

You could think of this as a stochastic version of case weights without the compactness.

## Pros and Cons

### Pros

- Computationally fast and simple.

### Cons

- Could give issues with space for large data sets.
- Solves tasks that could be better handled with other methods.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the `ames` data set for these examples.
The `MS_Zoning` variable is imbalanced, so we take the two largest classes to get a clean two-class problem to work with.
The same data set is used throughout this section so the methods can be compared against each other.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

We are using numeric predictors only because most of the other methods in this section require it.
Up-sampling itself has no such restriction, since it copies whole rows.

{themis} provides `step_upsample()`, which has the implementation for up-sampling.

```{r}
#| label: step_upsample
upsample_rec <- recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_upsample(MS_Zoning)

upsample_res <- upsample_rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

upsample_res |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

The minority class has been sampled with replacement until it matches the majority class.
Note that no new values were invented, the added rows are duplicates of rows that were already there.

```{r}
#| label: step_upsample-duplicates
upsample_res |>
  count(Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath, sort = TRUE)
```

It includes the `over_ratio` argument to only partially update the data set.

```{r}
#| label: step_upsample-over_ratio
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_upsample(MS_Zoning, over_ratio = 0.5) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

{imblearn} provides `RandomOverSampler()` for up-sampling.

Note that the samplers in {imblearn} do not follow the `fit()` and `transform()` pattern used elsewhere in this book.
Because they change the number of rows, they expose `fit_resample()` instead, which returns both the predictors and the outcome.

```{python}
#| label: randomoversampler
from imblearn.over_sampling import RandomOverSampler

X_res, y_res = RandomOverSampler(random_state=1234).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

The `sampling_strategy` argument plays the same role as `over_ratio` does in {themis}.

```{python}
#| label: randomoversampler-sampling_strategy
X_res, y_res = RandomOverSampler(
    sampling_strategy=0.5, random_state=1234).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

Because `fit_resample()` is not a transformer, a sampler cannot go into a regular {sklearn} `Pipeline`.
{imblearn} provides its own `Pipeline` that knows how to handle them.

```{python}
#| label: imblearn-pipeline
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('upsample', RandomOverSampler(random_state=1234)),
    ('scale', StandardScaler()),
    ('model', LogisticRegression()),
])

pipe.fit(X, y)
pipe.predict(X)[:5]
```

This pipeline is worth a closer look, because it encodes something the rest of this section depends on.
The sampler runs when you call `fit()`, and is skipped entirely when you call `predict()`.
That is what we want, since re-balancing is something we do to the training data to help the model learn, not something we do to data we want predictions for.
{themis} encodes the same idea with the `skip = TRUE` default that all of its steps carry.
